title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith
era: 1776 (An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations)
openingChapterLabel: Book I, Chapter 1 — Of the Division of Labour
openingText: The greatest improvements in the productive power of labour, and most of the skill, dexterity, and judgment with which labour is anywhere directed or applied, seem to have resulted from the division of labour. Let me take an example from a very trivial manufacture, but one in which the division of labour has very often been remarked upon: the trade of the pin-maker. A worker not trained in this business could scarcely, with his utmost effort, make one pin in a day, and certainly could not make twenty. But the work is now divided into about eighteen distinct operations, and I have seen a small factory where ten men, each performing two or three of them, could make among them upwards of forty-eight thousand pins in a day. Had they all worked separately and independently, they certainly could not each have made twenty pins a day, and perhaps not even one.
about:
Adam Smith published An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations in 1776, after roughly a decade of work and a long preparation that included his earlier book, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, and his years as a moral philosopher at Glasgow. It is not a pamphlet for or against any policy of the day but a systematic attempt to explain something that had never been explained: why some nations are rich and others poor, and what actually produces the steady growth of a people's wealth over time. Smith builds the answer from the ground up, beginning with a single pin factory and ending with the taxation and debts of whole states.

The argument runs in five books. Book I traces the division of labour, the origin of money, and the forces that fix the price of things and split that price into wages, profit, and rent. Book II turns to stock and capital — how it is accumulated, lent, and employed, and why productive labour matters more than unproductive. Book III tells the historical story of how wealth advanced in Europe after the fall of Rome, through the slow rise of cities and commerce. Book IV is a sustained attack on the mercantile system — the trade restraints, bounties, and colonial monopolies built on the confusion of money with wealth — and a shorter critique of the agricultural systems that opposed it. Book V deals with the expenses and revenue of the sovereign: the duties of defence, justice, and public works, and the principles by which taxes ought to be raised. It is the founding text of modern economics, and it reads less like a treatise than like a mind taking an entire commercial society apart to see how each piece moves the others.

angleCards.title: The pin factory and productivity.
angleCards.text: Book I opens with the division of labour, and the famous pin-maker is the whole book in miniature. Ten men split into eighteen operations make tens of thousands of pins a day; working alone, none could make twenty. Smith then asks where the limit lies — why the division of labour is bounded by the extent of the market, and why navigable water, not virtue, decided which nations grew rich first.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Smith's account of the division of labour in Book I — the pin factory, the three sources of its power, and his claim that it is limited only by the size of the market.

angleCards.title: Self-interest and the invisible hand.
angleCards.text: Smith's most quoted idea is that we get our dinner not from the butcher's kindness but from his self-love, and that an individual seeking only his own gain is 'led by an invisible hand' to an end he never intended. The phrase appears exactly once, deep in Book IV's attack on trade restraints. Read it in its place and notice how guarded and conditional Smith actually is.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the self-interest passages in their context — the butcher and baker in Book I, the single 'invisible hand' line in Book IV — and judge how far Smith actually pushes the claim.

angleCards.title: The case against the mercantile system.
angleCards.text: Book IV is the polemical heart of the book. Smith dismantles the mercantile system piece by piece: the confusion of gold with wealth, the restraints on imports, the bounties, the treaties of commerce, and above all the colonial monopolies. This is the argument that made the book a weapon in real political fights from its first year in print.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to work through Smith's critique of mercantilism in Book IV — what he says is wrong with import restraints, bounties, and colonial monopoly, and what he proposes in their place.

angleCards.title: The duties and the funding of the state.
angleCards.text: Book V is where Smith says what governments are for and how they should pay for it. He sets out three duties of the sovereign — defence, justice, and the public works that no private person will build — and then lays down four maxims of taxation: equality, certainty, convenience, and economy. Read closely and notice how much room he leaves for the state.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Book V on the role of the state — the three duties of the sovereign and the four maxims of taxation — and see where Smith draws the line between public and private.

cast.name: The Division of Labour
cast.description: The force Smith puts first and treats as the origin of nearly all productive power. Splitting a task among many specialised hands multiplies output through greater dexterity, time saved in switching jobs, and the machines that specialisation invites. Its reach is bounded only by the extent of the market, which is why commerce concentrated first along coasts and navigable rivers. The whole structure of the book grows out of this opening idea.

cast.name: Self-Interest and the Invisible Hand
cast.description: Smith's account of how a commercial society holds together without anyone directing it. We rely on the butcher, brewer, and baker not from their benevolence but from their regard to their own interest, and each pursuing his own gain is, in Smith's single use of the phrase, 'led by an invisible hand' to promote an end that was no part of his intention. He is sceptical of merchants who claim to trade for the public good. The idea is more careful and more hedged than its later fame suggests.

cast.name: Labour as the Measure of Value
cast.description: Smith's attempt to find a real, stable measure of what things are worth, set out in Book I's chapters on price. The real price of anything, he argues, is the toil and trouble of acquiring it; money prices only express that real cost imperfectly. The price of every commodity finally resolves into some combination of wages, profit, and rent. This is the analysis later economists built on and quarrelled with for a century.

cast.name: Stock and Capital
cast.description: The subject of Book II. Once labour is divided, work cannot go on until a stock of goods and tools has been gathered in advance, and the growth of a nation's wealth depends on how that stock is accumulated and employed. Smith separates productive labour, which adds to the stock, from unproductive labour, which consumes it, and traces how capital is lent at interest and directed into agriculture, manufactures, and trade. Saving, not spending, is what enlarges it.

cast.name: The Mercantile System
cast.description: The body of policy Smith spends Book IV demolishing. It rests on the mistake of identifying a nation's wealth with its hoard of gold and silver, and from that mistake flows a tangle of import restraints, bounties, monopoly trading companies, and colonial controls. Smith argues these enrich particular merchants at the expense of the whole society and of consumers above all. Naming and dismantling this system is the book's most directly political work.

cast.name: The Sovereign
cast.description: Smith's account of legitimate government, set out in Book V. The sovereign has three duties: to defend the society from outside attack, to administer justice and protect each member from the injustice of others, and to erect the public works and institutions that benefit everyone but pay no private person to build. To fund them Smith offers four maxims of taxation — equality, certainty, convenience, and economy — and a hard look at public debt. He is a critic of mercantilism, not an opponent of the state.

acclaim.quote: In the year 1776, Adam Smith published his Wealth of Nations, which, looking at its ultimate results, is probably the most important book that has ever been written.
acclaim.context: History of Civilization in England, Vol. I, 1857

acclaim.quote: The Wealth of Nations is a stupendous palace erected upon the granite of self-interest.
acclaim.context: "Smith's Travels on the Ship of State," History of Political Economy 3:2 (1971); repr. in Essays on Adam Smith, 1975

acclaim.quote: The life of almost everyone in England — perhaps of everyone — is different and better in consequence of it.
acclaim.context: "Adam Smith as a Person," Fortnightly Review, 1876; repr. in Biographical Studies, 1881

whyItMatters.title: The Division of Labour and Productivity
whyItMatters.body: The book opens on a question that still organises economics: why can a modern society produce so vastly more than a primitive one with the same number of hands? Smith's answer is the division of labour. Split a task among specialised workers and output multiplies through three channels — each worker grows more dexterous at one operation, no time is lost switching between jobs, and the narrowed focus invites the machines that shorten the work further. The pin factory makes the point concretely: ten men divided into eighteen operations make tens of thousands of pins a day, where each working alone could scarcely make one. Smith then bounds the idea — the division of labour can go no further than the extent of the market, which is why specialisation and improvement appeared first along coasts and navigable rivers rather than in the landlocked interior. The argument is the foundation on which the whole book is built, and it runs straight through to the assembly line and the global supply chain that move a phone from a dozen countries onto a desk.

whyItMatters.title: Self-Interest, Markets, and the Invisible Hand
whyItMatters.body: Smith asks how a society in which everyone specialises and no one can supply their own wants manages to feed and clothe itself without any central direction. His answer is exchange driven by self-interest: it is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. In the book's single, carefully placed use of the phrase, an individual who employs his capital only for his own gain is 'led by an invisible hand' to promote an end — the wealth of the whole society — that formed no part of his intention. Smith is no naive cheerleader for merchants; he warns repeatedly that they conspire against the public and dress private advantage as public good. The passage is far more guarded than its reputation, and that gap between the careful text and the slogan it became is exactly why the chapters on price and exchange reward a first-hand reading. Every present-day argument about whether markets coordinate better than planners starts here.

whyItMatters.title: The Duties and the Limits of the State
whyItMatters.body: Book V sets out what governments are for and how they should be paid for, and it is the part of Smith most often misremembered. He assigns the sovereign three duties: defending the society against outside force, administering justice so that no member is oppressed by another, and erecting the public works and institutions that serve everyone but that no private person would find it profitable to build. To fund these he lays down four maxims of taxation that are still quoted in tax policy — that taxes should fall in proportion to ability, be certain rather than arbitrary, be levied when and how it is convenient to pay, and cost as little as possible to collect beyond what they bring the state. Smith is a critic of the mercantile system's monopolies, not an enemy of public provision, and he is blunt about the corrosive danger of public debt. The book remains the reference point whenever a finance ministry argues about what the state should provide and how fairly the bill is shared.
